concept.name: Hallucination
concept.definition: The generation by a language model of content that is fluent and plausible but factually incorrect or unsupported by any source — including fabricated facts, citations, and data. NIST and industry glossaries increasingly prefer the term 'confabulation'; hallucination remains the widely used name.
concept.intuition: The model is a confident storyteller optimizing for plausible text, not a database: when it does not know, it often makes something up that sounds right rather than saying so.
concept.mechanics: Autoregressive generation samples tokens by learned statistical patterns; nothing in the objective guarantees factual grounding, so gaps in parametric knowledge are filled with high-probability but unverified continuations. Grounding, retrieval augmentation, and constrained decoding reduce but do not eliminate the phenomenon.
concept.failure_modes: Worst exactly where verification is hardest: rare facts, precise numbers, citations, and fast-changing domains such as market data or regulation. Hallucinated outputs are also self-consistent and confident, so they pass casual inspection.
concept.misconceptions: Hallucination is not a bug that a bigger model fully fixes, and retrieval augmentation does not eliminate it. It is also not 'lying' or intent — the model has no belief state; it is a structural property of next-token prediction.
concept.example: Asked for the exact tick value of a niche futures contract, a model confidently states a plausible but wrong dollar figure; only checking the exchange rulebook (grounding) catches the error.

citations.source: Google for Developers, 'Machine Learning Glossary' (entries: hallucination / confabulation)
